segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The council meets in the back room of the Last Coal to toast the open road. Nobody has touched the toast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The door bangs. Bree Tallow comes in out of the cold with two small goblins wrapped in her own shawl.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The bigger one pushes the smaller behind her and shows you her teeth. She's shaking too hard to make it frightening.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Halden doesn't reach for the ledger in front of him. He doesn't need to. He has carried those numbers for years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nobody drinks the toast. When the council goes home, the two small goblins are asleep by Bree's fire, and the room is very quiet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Night in the hills. The clan's camp is empty: cold fire pits, a dropped doll, tent poles with nothing hung on them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Dagna carries Mother Skarrow up the path herself, wrapped in a guard's cloak. She won't let anyone else take a turn.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the end the words are short ones. Her name. Forty winters. A clan that ate, for as long as she could make it eat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nobody knows it. The wind goes through the empty tents, and for a moment it almost sounds like humming.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You speak the old farewell, the one for chiefs. Somewhere in the dark above the camp, someone answers it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The cairn is small. Dagna sets a guard's spear on top of it, point down, the way soldiers mark an enemy they respected.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The lantern on the pier gutters. When it steadies, the Stranger is gone, and Rook is leaning on the rail where they stood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Before dawn, two of Dagna's guards stand on the third pier with lanterns. The ember stays in the riverbed, keeping Emberwick warm a while longer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At a frozen shrine halfway up the pass, someone is singing to the dead. Lark sits cross-legged in the snow, and the risen pilgrims stand quite still to listen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Lark looks past you, and the song stops.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Hooded Stranger stands at the edge of the shrine. Snow settles on their hood and does not melt.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wind throws snow across the shrine. When it clears, the Stranger is gone, and their footprints with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Lark climbs the last stair behind you, for once without a song.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Behind you, Lark's hand has stopped on the strings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Lark sets one foot on the rim of the well and sings, low and clear, until the square goes quiet.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: The bridge is ours again. I keep telling myself that's what I wanted.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: Goblins at the granary gate, and nobody dead. I'll take it. I'll take it gladly.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: Friends. The road east is open, the carts are crossing, and Emberwick will eat this winter. To that, and to our heroes.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: Then the granary can spare a sack. A small one. We must think of the spring.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: A mayor does a great many sums, friend, and none of them are cheerful. That's all.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: Because the ground is cooling. The ember under the ford is going out, and I have known it for six years.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: Every winter the warm fields give a little less. I measured it. I said nothing, because half the town would have packed and gone.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: So I locked the grain and let the hills go hungry, and when they came down for it we called them thieves. And then we sent spears.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: Yes. From tomorrow, in the open, with witnesses. I am done hiding the count.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: The granaries open tomorrow. A sack in four goes up the hill, to whoever will take it.

segments.speaker: townsfolk_farmer
segments.text: They say the old goblin woman died on the bridge. Road's open. Doesn't feel like winning.

segments.speaker: townsfolk_farmer
segments.text: Goblins on the hill, grain going up the path. Odd neighbours. Better than dead ones.

segments.speaker: townsfolk_farmer
segments.text: They found something under the river, they say. The field by the docks froze the same night.

segments.speaker: townsfolk_farmer
segments.text: Mayor knew the ground was cooling. Six years he knew. I'd have planted differently.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: The docks went cold the night you brought it up. If that thing kept Emberwick warm, I need to know what we do now.

segments.speaker: halden_varrow
segments.text: The bridge is open. The road is open. I ought to be relieved, and I keep seeing her on the planks.

superseded.speaker: narrator
superseded.text: By the next market day, ember shards are selling for a copper apiece. Every hearth in Emberwick burns a little brighter.
